lead: The geometric and negative binomial distributions answer a waiting question. You repeat independent yes/no trials with the same success probability p and count trials until a fixed number of successes arrives. The geometric stops at the first success; the negative binomial stops at the r-th success. Cricket wickets per over, quality checks for defective items, and insurance claims use this count. The key number is the trial on which the required success lands, not the number of failures.
prereq: You need: independent Bernoulli trials and the binomial count from Chapter 3.1, plus conditional probability from Unit 2.

blocks.text: Toss a biased coin until the first head. Each toss is an independent trial with success probability p, and T is the trial number of that first success. For the first success to land on trial k, the first k − 1 trials must all fail and trial k must succeed. Independence multiplies the probabilities. Put q = 1 − p, the failure probability. The geometric pmf is below. The support starts at 1; T = 0 is not a trial count.

blocks.where: T is the number of trials up to and including the first success; p is the success probability on one trial; (1 − p) is the failure probability.

blocks.text: The probabilities sum to 1: Σ<sub>k=1</sub><sup>∞</sup> (1 − p)<sup>k − 1</sup> p = 1. Its mean is E[T] = 1/p. If p = 0.3, you expect 1/0.3 ≈ 3.33 overs for the first wicket. Its variance is Var(T) = (1 − p)/p², so a small p gives a long and highly variable wait. Some syllabi call this the waiting-time distribution. If X counts failures before the first success, then P(X = x) = (1 − p)<sup>x</sup> p for x = 0, 1, 2, ..., with mean (1 − p)/p. That X is T − 1.

Fix r, the required number of successes. Let T be the trial number on which the r-th success lands. Trial k is a success, and among the first k − 1 trials there are exactly r − 1 successes. Choose those r − 1 positions in C(k − 1, r − 1) ways. The probability of any one such pattern is p<sup>r − 1</sup>(1 − p)<sup>k − r</sup>, and trial k adds one more p. So the negative binomial pmf is below. Its support starts at k = r.
P(T = k) = C(k − 1, r − 1) p<sup>r</sup> (1 − p)<sup>k − r</sup>, k = r, r + 1, ...
blocks.where: T is the trial number of the r-th success; r is the fixed number of successes; p is the success probability on one trial; C(k − 1, r − 1) is the number of ways to place the first r − 1 successes among the first k − 1 trials.

blocks.text: Its mean is E[T] = r/p and its variance is Var(T) = r(1 − p)/p². The geometric is the r = 1 case. Some syllabi call this the Pascal distribution. If Y counts failures before the r-th success, then Y = T − r, P(Y = y) = C(y + r − 1, y) p<sup>r</sup>(1 − p)<sup>y</sup>, and E[Y] = r(1 − p)/p.

The geometric distribution is discrete memoryless. For nonnegative integers m and n, P(T > m + n | T > m) = P(T > n). After m failures, the chance of n more failures is the same as at the start. Proof: P(T > m) = (1 − p)<sup>m</sup> and P(T > m + n) = (1 − p)<sup>m + n</sup>; their ratio is (1 − p)<sup>n</sup>. A bowler who has not taken a wicket for 10 overs does not get a 'due' wicket: if overs are independent, p stays 0.3.

The negative binomial is a sum of r independent geometric waiting times with the same p, so its mean and variance are r times those of the geometric. Use these models for quality inspection until r defective items, insurance claims until r claims, and cricket wickets per over when overs are independent. For continuous waiting, see Chapter 3.5.

figure.caption: Independent overs feed two waiting counts: the geometric for the first wicket and the negative binomial for the second. Notice that the second probability uses C(4,1), the choice of which of the first four overs held the first wicket.

spec.title: Waiting for wickets
spec.aria: Flow from independent overs to the geometric first-wicket probability and negative binomial second-wicket probability.

examples.question: A bowler takes a wicket with probability 0.3 each over, independently. Find P(first wicket in the 4th over) and P(second wicket in the 5th over).
steps: Set p = 0.3 and q = 1 − p = 0.7. Let T<sub>1</sub> be the over of the first wicket.
First wicket in over 4: overs 1 to 3 have no wicket, and over 4 has a wicket. P(T<sub>1</sub> = 4) = q³p = 0.7³ × 0.3.
Second wicket in over 5: over 5 has a wicket, and among overs 1 to 4 there is exactly 1 wicket. Choose its over in C(4,1) = 4 ways. P(T<sub>2</sub> = 5) = C(4,1) p² q³.
examples.answer: P(first wicket in the 4th over) = 0.1029 and P(second wicket in the 5th over) = 0.1235, about 10.29% and 12.35%.
examples.check:
import math
p = 0.3
q = 1 - p
first = q**3 * p
second = math.comb(4, 1) * p**2 * q**3
print(round(first, 4))
print(round(second, 4))

traps: Counting failures instead of trials: the geometric pmf (1 − p)<sup>k − 1</sup>p has support k = 1, 2, ..., so P(T = 0) is not allowed. If Y counts failures before the first success, then P(Y = y) = (1 − p)<sup>y</sup>p with y = 0, 1, 2, ...
Using C(k, r) instead of C(k − 1, r − 1) in the negative binomial. Trial k is fixed as the r-th success, so only the first k − 1 trials are arranged.
Forgetting that the negative binomial support starts at k = r. Values below r have probability 0.
Treating the memoryless property as 'the next trial must succeed after many failures'. It says the conditional chance stays p, not that a success is due.
Using the failure-count mean (1 − p)/p as the trial-count mean. The geometric trial-count mean is 1/p.

quiz.q: State the geometric pmf for T, the trial number of the first success with success probability p.
quiz.a: P(T = k) = (1 − p)<sup>k − 1</sup>p for k = 1, 2, 3, ...; T is the trial number of the first success and p is the success probability on one trial.

quiz.q: Explain why the negative binomial uses C(k − 1, r − 1) and not C(k, r).
quiz.a: Trial k must be the r-th success, so it is fixed. The remaining r − 1 successes are placed among the first k − 1 trials, giving C(k − 1, r − 1) arrangements. C(k, r) would allow trial k to be a failure.

quiz.q: A machine produces a defective item with probability 0.1 independently. Find P(first defective on item 5).
With p = 0.4, find the mean and variance of T, the trial number of the third success.
A student says: 'The bowler has not taken a wicket for 6 overs, so a wicket is due.' Use the memoryless property to correct it with p = 0.3.
quiz.a: After 6 failed overs, P(T > 7 | T > 6) = P(T > 1) = 0.7, so the next over still has wicket probability 0.3. Past failures do not raise p when overs are independent.

quiz.q: Write the relation between the geometric and negative binomial distributions.
quiz.a: The geometric is the negative binomial with r = 1: waiting for the first success is waiting for the 1st success.

quiz.q: If X counts failures before the first success, write P(X = x), its mean and variance, and relate X to T, the trial number of the first success.
quiz.a: P(X = x) = (1 − p)<sup>x</sup>p for x = 0, 1, 2, ...; mean = (1 − p)/p; variance = (1 − p)/p². X = T − 1, so E[T] = 1/p.

beyond: Not for the exam. In reliability and queueing, the geometric is the discrete counterpart of the exponential, and the negative binomial appears when a system needs r repairs before replacement. In modern data science, negative binomial regression is used for over-dispersed counts, such as RNA sequencing reads or insurance claim counts, where the Poisson variance is too small. Search for 'negative binomial regression', 'overdispersion' and 'Pascal distribution'.
